```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 90)
# The evaluated examples run against a local replay of responses recorded from
# the production API (tests/testthat/fixtures/recorded, tools/record_fixtures.R):
# no network and no login at build time; the outputs are real API outputs,
# including the export (submitted, followed, downloaded and read back).
soil <- soilhub:::replay_session()
```

```{r}
library(soilhub)
```

`soil_observations()` reads data directly into R. For very large selections
(a whole dataset, a continent) the hub prepares a **file** instead: an
**export**. This guide shows how to size a selection, what happens when it
is too large, and how to export, download and read the files. It assumes
you have signed in as shown in `vignette("soilhub", package = "soilhub")`.
The outputs were recorded from the Global Soil Data Hub API in October 2026.

## The limits of the server

The server says how much it accepts in its capabilities:

```{r}
limits <- soil_capabilities(soil)$limits
limits$max_sync_observations
limits$max_export_observations
```

- a direct read (`soil_observations()`) may hold up to 1,000,000
  observations (measured values);
- an export may hold up to 10,000,000.

## Size the selection first

`soil_summary()` counts a selection without transferring it. For WoSIS in
Kenya:

```{r}
kenya <- soil_summary(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", country = "KEN")
kenya$observation_count
```

About 46,000 observations: well below the limit, so a direct read works. A
rule of thumb: below about 200,000 observations read directly; above, use an
export (it is also the way to get files for a GIS).

## When a selection is too large

If you ask for too much, the server refuses and the package stops with an
error that explains what to do. Here we ask for every dataset of the hub,
with no filter. We use `tryCatch()` to keep the error in a variable instead
of stopping:

```{r}
result <- tryCatch(
  soil_observations(soil, max_rows = 5),
  error = function(e) e
)
class(result)[1]
```

The error is a `soilhub_load_limit_error`. Its message says why and gives
the way out:

```{r}
cat(conditionMessage(result))
```

The selection holds more than a million observations. You can narrow it
(an area with `bbox` or `country`, fewer `datasets` or `variables`) or
export it.

## Export a selection

`soil_export()` sends the selection to the server, waits while the file is
written, downloads it and unzips it in a folder (`dir`). Here: WoSIS around
Vancouver (Canada) as CSV, checked every 2 seconds, saved in a temporary
folder (use your own folder, for example `dir = "exports"`).

```{r}
vancouver <- c(-123.3, 49.0, -122.9, 49.4)
e <- soil_export(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", bbox = vancouver,
                 format = "csv", poll = 2, dir = tempdir())
```

```{r}
e
```

The export is `completed`. It holds 4 features (profile sites) and 12
horizon rows, with 30 observations, in three files: the places
(`features.csv`), the measurements (`observations.csv`) and a description
(`metadata.json`). The **job id** (`exp_...`) identifies the export; the
file stays on the server for a week (`Expires`).

## Read the files back

`soil_export_read()` reads the measurements into a table, with the same
columns as `soil_observations()`:

```{r}
horizons <- soil_export_read(e)
nrow(horizons)
```

```{r}
horizons[, c("horizon_name", "upper_depth_cm", "lower_depth_cm", "organic_carbon")]
```

Unlike the direct read of the other guides (limited to 5 rows), the export
holds **every** horizon of the selection: 12 horizons of 3 profiles.

The places are read with `what = "features"`:

```{r}
places <- soil_export_read(e, what = "features")
nrow(places)
```

Four places but only three profiles with horizons: one site has no
measurements (see `vignette("first-layer", package = "soilhub")`).

As for any read, `soil_citations()` tells you what to cite:

```{r}
soil_citations(horizons)$citation_text
```

## Export now, download later

A large export can take minutes. With `wait = FALSE` the function returns
at once; keep the job id, it is the only way to find the export again
(these calls are not run here).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
e <- soil_export(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", country = "BRA",
                 format = "gpkg", wait = FALSE)
e$job_id
#> [1] "exp_20261020_..."
```

Later, even in another R session:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
e <- soil_export_wait(soil, "exp_20261020_...")
e <- soil_export_download(soil, e, dir = "exports")
horizons <- soil_export_read(e)
```

## Files for a GIS

The formats are `"csv"`, `"tsv"`, `"geojson"`, `"gpkg"` (GeoPackage) and
`"shp"` (Shapefile, only for the places: `content = "features"`). The
GeoPackage and Shapefile need the package `sf` to be read in R, and open
directly in QGIS or ArcGIS (these calls are not run here):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gpkg <- soil_export(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", country = "KEN",
                    format = "gpkg", dir = "exports")

shp <- soil_export(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", country = "KEN",
                   format = "shp", content = "features", dir = "exports")
```

## Let the package switch to an export

With `too_large = "export"` a read that the server refuses as too large is
exported, downloaded and read back for you, with the same result as a direct
read (this call is not run here):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
x <- soil_observations(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", too_large = "export")
```

If you already have the error, `soil_export_from_error()` exports the same
selection:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
e <- soil_export_from_error(soil, result, format = "gpkg", dir = "exports")
```

```{r teardown, include = FALSE}
soilhub:::replay_stop(soil)
```
